# Video Generation {#sec-video-generation}

Video generation is a *generalisation* of image generation: a model
samples a clip
$\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times 3}$ from a
distribution $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{V} \mid \mathbf{c})$ conditioned on
some control signal $\mathbf{c}$ — most commonly a text prompt, but
also an image (image-to-video), a previous clip (extension), a
reference identity (subject-driven generation), or a structured pose
/ depth / camera trajectory (control-net style generation).

An image is the degenerate case $T = 1$, so anything that works for
image generation is a candidate for video. But the temporal axis adds
two new requirements that change the engineering substantially:

- **Temporal consistency.** Independently generated frames flicker:
  identities drift, lighting jumps, objects re-appear with different
  textures. Modelling joint dependencies across frames is what
  separates a real video model from a slideshow of images.
- **Sequence length.** A 5-second 720p clip at 24 FPS has
  $120 \times 720 \times 1280 \times 3 \approx 3.3 \times 10^8$
  pixels. Even with a 8 × 8 × 4 latent VAE, a denoiser operates on
  $\sim 10^6$ tokens per clip. Memory and compute become the dominant
  engineering constraints; almost every video-generation paper of
  2022–2026 is a memory trick in some form.

The 2022–2026 landscape splits naturally along two axes:

1. **What is the denoiser?** *U-Net + temporal layers* (the inherited
   image-diffusion stack, 2022–2024) vs *Diffusion Transformer (DiT)*
   (Peebles & Xie [@peebles2023dit]; the dominant 2024–2026 design,
   used by Sora, Stable Video Diffusion 3, CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo).
2. **How is video conditioning added?** Three families, corresponding
   to *how much training* the video data sees:
    - **Train from scratch** on video data (VDM, Imagen Video, Sora,
      CogVideoX).
    - **Fine-tune a pretrained image model** by adding temporal
      layers, sometimes only training those (Make-a-Video, Video
      LDM / Align-Your-Latents, Stable Video Diffusion).
    - **Train-free adaptation** of a pretrained image model — no
      weight updates, only inference-time tricks (Text2Video-Zero).

This chapter follows that taxonomy. We first review the diffusion
fundamentals (@sec-gen-diffusion), then walk through the three
families in order of increasing training cost (@sec-gen-three),
discuss the orthogonal *autoregressive* line (@sec-gen-ar), survey
the closed-source flagships (@sec-gen-flagships) and the
open-weights landscape (@sec-gen-open), and close with the
evaluation question (@sec-gen-eval).

::: {.callout-note}
The focus of these notes is video *understanding*. This chapter is
included so that a video-VLM engineer reading the rest of the book
has the vocabulary to follow a generation paper, recognise the
shared components (VAE, T5/CLIP encoder, DiT backbone), and pick a
sensible evaluation setup. It is not a substitute for a full
generative-models text.
:::


## Diffusion Fundamentals {#sec-gen-diffusion}

Almost every video generator in this chapter is a diffusion model.
This section recaps the minimum prerequisite vocabulary. Readers
familiar with image diffusion can skim straight to @sec-gen-three.

### Denoising Diffusion {#sec-gen-ddpm}

Diffusion models [@ho2020ddpm; @sohl2015deepunsup] define a forward
*noising* process that gradually turns a real sample
$\mathbf{x}_0$ into Gaussian noise $\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0,
\mathbf{I})$ over $T$ steps:

$$
q(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{t-1}) =
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_t; \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t-1},
\beta_t\mathbf{I})
$$ {#eq-diffusion-forward}

with a variance schedule $\{\beta_t\}_{t=1}^{T}$. The forward
process has a closed-form marginal,
$\mathbf{x}_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,\mathbf{x}_0 +
\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ with $\bar{\alpha}_t
\;=\; \prod_{s \leq t} (1 - \beta_s)$. A *denoiser*
$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c})$ is trained
to predict the noise added at step $t$, optimising

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}}(\theta) \;=\;
\mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
\bigl[ \| \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c}) -
\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \|_2^2 \bigr].
$$ {#eq-diffusion-loss}

Sampling reverses the chain: starting from $\mathbf{x}_T \sim
\mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})$ and iterating
$\mathbf{x}_t \to \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$ using the predicted noise. A 1000-
step DDPM trajectory is wasteful; DDIM [@song2021ddim] replaces it
with a deterministic ODE solve and 20–50 steps are typical in 2024–
2026. Faster solvers (DPM-Solver-2 / 3, UniPC) push this to single
digits.

### Classifier-Free Guidance {.unnumbered}

Almost all video generators use classifier-free guidance (CFG)
[@ho2021cfg]: train the denoiser jointly with conditional and
unconditional inputs (drop the conditioning $\mathbf{c}$ with
probability ~10 %), then at sampling time blend them:

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{c}) \;=\;
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, \varnothing)
\;+\; w \bigl[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{c})
- \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, \varnothing)\bigr]
$$ {#eq-cfg}

with guidance scale $w > 1$ (typically 4–7.5 for image, 6–9 for
video). CFG is the lever that trades sample diversity for prompt
fidelity.

### Latent Diffusion {.unnumbered}

Running diffusion on raw pixels is prohibitively expensive for
video. Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) [@rombach2022ldm] compress
$\mathbf{x}$ to a low-dimensional latent
$\mathbf{z} = \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})$ via a frozen VAE, run
diffusion in $\mathbf{z}$-space, and decode back at the end via
$\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_0)$. For video this
matters even more: a *3D VAE* (space + time, typically 8 × 8 × 4
compression — CogVideoX 1.5 uses 16 × 16 × 4, Sora uses an
"undisclosed but aggressive" 3D VAE) reduces a 16 × 720 × 1280 ×
3 clip to a 4 × 90 × 160 × 16 latent — a 24× memory saving.

### Text Conditioning {.unnumbered}

Text prompts enter the denoiser via cross-attention from a frozen
language encoder. The three dominant choices in 2024–2026:

- **CLIP-text** (OpenAI / OpenCLIP) — fast, strong on short prompts,
  weak on compositional language. The default for the Stable
  Diffusion 1.x / 2.x line.
- **T5-XXL / Flan-T5-XXL** [@raffel2020t5] — the heavyweight in
  Imagen, Imagen Video, DeepFloyd-IF, Sora, and CogVideoX. Excellent
  at long prompts and compositions, expensive to run.
- **LLM-as-text-encoder** — direct hidden states from a Llama-3-class
  LLM, often distilled into a smaller adapter. Used by HunyuanVideo
  and several 2025 open-weights models; trades T5's robustness for
  better instruction-following.

### Denoiser architectures: U-Net vs DiT {.unnumbered}

For image diffusion, the original choice was a *U-Net* with cross-
attention to text [@ronneberger2015unet; @rombach2022ldm]. Peebles &
Xie [@peebles2023dit] showed that a **Diffusion Transformer (DiT)**
— a plain transformer over a tokenised latent grid — scales better
and beats the U-Net once data and compute are abundant. The video
field has followed the same trajectory:

- 2022–2023 video models (VDM, Make-a-Video, Video LDM, Stable Video
  Diffusion) used **U-Net + factorised space-time attention or
  3D convolutions**.
- 2024 onwards (Sora, CogVideoX, Mochi-1, HunyuanVideo, Wan-2.1,
  LTX-Video, Open-Sora-Plan) uses **DiT-style transformers** over a
  3D-VAE latent.

The DiT wins for the same reason it does in image generation: a plain
transformer scales cleanly, parameter-shares across all spatial and
temporal positions, and benefits from every infrastructure
improvement made for LLMs (FlashAttention, pipeline parallelism,
sequence parallelism, etc.).


## Three Families of Video Generation {#sec-gen-three}

The video-diffusion approaches of 2022–2026 fall into three families
distinguished by how much *video* training they do.

### Family 1 — Train from Scratch on Video {#sec-gen-scratch}

The cleanest baseline: train a denoiser on video data only, with no
image pretraining. Used by the biggest closed flagships (Sora) and by
recent open-weights efforts that have the compute (CogVideoX,
HunyuanVideo). The early open-academic example is VDM.

#### Video Diffusion Models (VDM, 2022) {.unnumbered}

[VDM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.03458) [@ho2022vdm] (Ho et al.,
2022) introduced the modern video-diffusion template. The denoiser is
a **3D U-Net factorised over space and time**:

- Each *spatial 2D convolution* is extended to a "space-only 3D
  convolution" with kernel size $(1, 3, 3)$ — only the spatial axes
  see the kernel; frames are processed independently.
- Each *spatial self-attention layer* is left as is, but with the
  frames axis treated as a batch dimension.
- After every spatial self-attention block, a **temporal attention
  block** is inserted, with the spatial axes folded into the batch
  dimension. The temporal positional embedding is a *relative* one
  (no absolute notion of time, so the model works across arbitrary
  clip lengths).

This *factorised* design — spatial blocks operating on frames in
parallel, temporal blocks acting only across time — became the
canonical pattern. Almost every video diffusion model of 2022–2024
inherits it; the DiT variants of 2024–2026 generalise it with a
single transformer that attends across (t, h, w) jointly but still
often uses block-sparse masks that recover the factorised form for
compute efficiency.

#### Imagen Video (2022) {.unnumbered}

[Imagen Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02303) [@ho2022imagenvideo]
(Google, 2022) tackled the *resolution* problem: generating long,
high-resolution videos directly is too expensive, so use a *cascade*
of seven diffusion models that progressively refine spatial and
temporal resolution:

1. A **base** diffusion model produces a low-resolution, short clip
   (40 × 24 × 24, 16 frames at ~3 FPS).
2. Three **spatial super-resolution (SSR)** models progressively
   upscale: 24×24 → 80×80 → 240×240 → 720×720.
3. Three **temporal super-resolution (TSR)** models interpolate in
   time: 16 frames → 32 → 64 → 128 frames (≈5 s at 24 FPS).

Each stage is conditioned on T5-XXL text embeddings and on the
output of the previous stage. The base model is a 3D-conv U-Net with
spatio-temporal self-attention; the upsamplers use cheaper
alternatives — temporal *convolutions* instead of attention (linear
in frames, not quadratic) and *no* spatial attention at the highest
resolution (where it would dominate compute). The result was the
first text-to-video model widely regarded as "production quality" by
the standards of 2022, and it set the cascade template that Sora
later inherited.

#### Sora (2024) {.unnumbered}

[Sora](https://openai.com/sora/) [@openai2024sora] (OpenAI, Feb 2024)
is the headline closed-flagship that made transformer-based video
generation mainstream. Two architectural breaks with the 2022 line:

- **DiT denoiser.** Replace the 3D U-Net with a plain transformer.
- **3D space-time patches.** Instead of 2D patches from a single
  image, Sora extracts $p_t \times p_h \times p_w$ spacetime patches
  (e.g. $2 \times 16 \times 16$ pixels) from the 3D-VAE-compressed
  latent. Each patch becomes a token; the transformer applies self-
  attention across *all* spacetime tokens to model spatial and
  temporal dependencies *jointly* (rather than via the factorised
  pattern of VDM/Imagen Video).

The conditioning stack is standard — cross-attention from a T5-XXL
text encoder, with classifier-free guidance for sampling. The
training data and exact 3D-VAE design are not disclosed, but the
inferred recipe is: a high-compression-ratio 3D VAE (likely
$8 \times 8 \times 4$ or finer), a billion-parameter DiT, and
multi-aspect-ratio / multi-duration training so the same model
serves 5-second portrait clips and 60-second landscape clips. Sora 2
(2024) and the disclosed Wan, HunyuanVideo, Mochi, CogVideoX
designs follow the same pattern with smaller, public weights.

#### CogVideoX / CogVideoX 1.5 (Tsinghua + Zhipu AI, 2024) {.unnumbered}

[CogVideoX](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06072) [@yang2024cogvideox]
(Aug 2024, 1.5 released Nov 2024) is the canonical open-weights
*train-from-scratch* video DiT. Three contributions:

- **3D-VAE with $4 \times 8 \times 8$ compression** (1.5 raised this
  to $4 \times 16 \times 16$).
- **Expert Adaptive Layer Normalisation.** Conditioning signals
  (timestep, text) modulate the transformer through dedicated
  AdaLN "experts" rather than via cross-attention. This was
  influential — many 2024–2026 video DiTs followed.
- **Multi-resolution / multi-duration training** with bucketing,
  similar to Sora's inferred recipe but disclosed.

CogVideoX-5B (5 B-parameter DiT) and 1.5-5B are the most-used open
references for academic comparisons in 2025–2026.

### Family 2 — Fine-tune a Pretrained Image Model {#sec-gen-finetune}

The pragmatic majority of 2022–2024 work. Start from a strong image
diffusion model (Stable Diffusion 1.5 / 2.1, eDiff-I, IF) and *add*
temporal layers. Often only the new temporal layers are trained, with
the image weights kept frozen — this is cheap, the image model has
already learned visual priors, and the resulting generator inherits
the image model's compositional strength.

#### Make-A-Video (2022) {.unnumbered}

[Make-A-Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.14792)
[@singer2022makeavideo] (Meta, Sep 2022) — the first widely cited
example. Composition of three modules:

1. A *pretrained* text-to-image diffusion model (eDiff-I-class).
2. A **spatiotemporal super-resolution** model that upgrades the
   image generator to a video generator by adding *(2+1)D* layers:
    - **(2+1)D convolutions**: each pretrained 2D conv is followed
      by a new 1D temporal conv, initialised to the identity. The
      2D conv first generates a stack of frames in parallel; the
      1D conv smooths across time.
    - **(2+1)D attention**: each spatial attention layer is followed
      by a new temporal attention layer that attends only across
      frames at each spatial position.
3. A **frame interpolation** network that increases frame rate.

Only the new temporal modules are trained; the image weights stay
frozen, so the model inherits Make-a-Scene-class image quality at
roughly the training cost of a temporal-only model. The (2+1)D
factorisation became standard for years.

#### Video LDM / Align-Your-Latents (2023) {.unnumbered}

[Align-Your-Latents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08818)
[@blattmann2023videoldm] (Blattmann et al., 2023, NVIDIA / LMU
Munich) — the canonical *latent* variant of the Make-A-Video idea.
Build on a Stable-Diffusion-style LDM:

- **Insert temporal layers** (3D convolutions + temporal attention)
  *between* the frozen spatial layers of the image LDM.
- **Train only the temporal layers** with the spatial LDM weights
  frozen.
- Use a **personalised** decoder: the original LDM decoder produces
  flickering artefacts when frames are decoded independently, so a
  *video-aware* decoder is fine-tuned — temporal layers are added,
  spatial encoder weights are kept frozen, and the decoder is
  trained jointly with a reconstruction loss and a GAN-style 3D-conv
  patch discriminator that distinguishes real from generated video
  clips.

Video LDM is the template for **Stable Video Diffusion (SVD)**
[@blattmann2023svd] (Stability AI, Nov 2023), the most-downloaded
open-weights video model of 2023–2024. SVD trains the SD-2.1 U-Net
with added temporal layers on a curated 5-million-clip subset of the
LVD corpus and produces 14- or 25-frame 1024 × 576 clips. It is the
default *image-to-video* baseline in most 2024 papers.

### Family 3 — Train-Free Adaptation {#sec-gen-trainfree}

Inference-time tricks that produce video from a pretrained image
diffusion model with no weight updates. Cheap, fast, sufficient for
short demos, but lacking the realism of trained models. Useful
mainly as a baseline and for one-off effects.

#### Text2Video-Zero (2023) {.unnumbered}

[Text2Video-Zero](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13439)
[@khachatryan2023text2videozero] (Picsart AI Research, Mar 2023) — the
reference train-free method. Two tricks:

1. **Camera-motion noise initialisation.** Start with one random
   latent $\mathbf{z}_T$. Run a single DDIM backward step to denoise
   it slightly. Apply a sequence of *translations* to the resulting
   latent (simulating a panning camera). Then take a DDPM forward
   step to obtain a sequence of noised latents, each related to the
   first by a known linear shift in latent space. This injects
   coherent inter-frame motion at the noise level.
2. **Cross-frame attention.** Reprogram the U-Net's self-attention
   so that each frame's queries cross-attend (using the *image*
   model's pretrained Q, K, V matrices) to the *first* frame's
   keys and values. The first frame thus acts as an anchor for
   object identity and background.

The result is short, somewhat coherent video from a frozen image
diffusion model. Not competitive with trained models on benchmarks,
but a useful diagnostic — when an image diffusion model produces
better short clips with these tricks than a poorly-trained video
diffusion model produces with full training, the latter has
something wrong.


## Autoregressive Video Generation {#sec-gen-ar}

Orthogonal to the diffusion line is the **autoregressive (AR)**
approach: tokenise video into a sequence of discrete codes and
predict the next code. Two variants:

- **Discrete VAE / VQ-VAE tokenisation** [@vandenoord2017vqvae;
  @esser2021vqgan; @sun2024llamagen]. A VQ-VAE maps each clip to a
  sequence of integer codes from a fixed codebook (e.g. 16 384
  entries). A transformer is trained with a next-token-prediction
  loss on these codes; sampling decodes from codes back to pixels.
  The original VQ-VAE-based video generators (Video VQ-VAE, NUWA-XL)
  date to 2021–2022; the more capable modern examples are below.
- **Continuous AR with a diffusion head** [@li2024marsmar;
  @tian2024nextscale]. Predict the *parameters* of the next frame's
  distribution autoregressively, but parameterise that distribution
  as a small diffusion model. Hybrid; recent and less proven for
  video specifically.

The autoregressive line is appealing for two reasons:

- **Token interface unification with LLMs.** A video tokeniser turns
  video into the same token stream as text, so a single transformer
  can read a video and write a video — exactly the *understanding +
  generation* unification that Janus-Pro pursued in
  @sec-vlm-specialised.
- **Inherits LLM infrastructure.** Speculative decoding, prefix
  caching, FlashAttention, pipeline parallelism — every win the LLM
  community gets transfers for free.

The headline open-source examples:

- **VideoPoet** [@kondratyuk2024videopoet] (Google, Dec 2023). The
  first large-scale (~8B-param) autoregressive video LM. Predicts a
  unified stream of *image tokens + audio tokens + text tokens*,
  enabling text-to-video, image-to-video, video stylisation, and
  audio-to-video in a single model. Uses MAGVIT-v2 [@yu2024magvit2]
  as the video tokeniser, which crucially improved tokeniser quality
  to the point AR video matched diffusion on FVD.
- **LlamaGen** [@sun2024llamagen] (ByteDance, Jun 2024). Image-only
  but architecturally the cleanest demonstration: a vanilla LLaMA
  transformer with a high-quality VQ tokeniser produces images at
  Stable-Diffusion quality. The video extension is implicit in the
  Janus-Pro line — Janus-Pro [@chen2025januspro] uses the same VQ
  tokeniser approach for image generation, embedded in a unified
  understanding/generation transformer (see @sec-vlm-specialised).
- **MAGI-1, Cosmos-1** (NVIDIA, late 2024) — recent autoregressive
  video models for world simulation; smaller community footprint than
  the diffusion line but increasingly relevant for robotics and
  embodied AI.

As of mid-2026 the diffusion-DiT line is still ahead on raw video
quality (Sora, Veo 3, CogVideoX 1.5), but the AR + diffusion-head
hybrids are closing the gap, and the *unification* argument keeps
this line architecturally alive.


## Closed-Source Flagships {#sec-gen-flagships}

Brief mentions to anchor the architecture discussion in the public
state of the art. None of these have full disclosed weights but most
have technical reports.

- **Sora / Sora 2** [@openai2024sora] (OpenAI). The reference
  text-to-video DiT, 1080p, up to ~1 minute. Sora 2 (Sep 2024) adds
  synchronised audio generation and improved long-clip coherence.
- **Veo / Veo 2 / Veo 3** [@deepmind2024veo] (Google DeepMind).
  4K-capable, 8-second prompts with strong physics. Veo 3 (May 2025)
  added native audio (dialogue, sound effects) at video-generation
  time and now matches or exceeds Sora 2 on most evaluation axes.
- **Movie Gen** [@meta2024moviegen] (Meta, Oct 2024). 30B-parameter
  text-to-video DiT trained on a curated 100M-video corpus; also
  generates synced audio and allows *video editing* (text-guided
  edits to a given clip).
- **Genie / Genie 2 / Genie 3** [@bruce2024genie] (Google DeepMind).
  Action-conditioned world model — given an image, the model
  generates *playable* video where the user can control the agent.
  Conceptually distinct from the text-to-video flagships above —
  more an interactive world simulator than a film generator.
- **Runway Gen-3 / Gen-4, Pika 2.0, Luma Dream Machine** (2024–2025).
  Commercial generators with strong consumer features (motion
  brushes, style transfer, character LoRAs) and undisclosed
  architectural details.


## Open-Source Landscape (2024–2026) {#sec-gen-open}

The open-weights line has been moving extremely fast since
CogVideoX. The current shortlist, all DiT-based unless noted:

- **CogVideoX-2B / 5B / CogVideoX 1.5-5B** [@yang2024cogvideox]
  (Aug 2024 → Nov 2024) — see @sec-gen-scratch. 5 B-param DiT,
  Apache-2.0; the academic baseline.
- **Mochi 1** [@genmo2024mochi] (Genmo, Oct 2024) — 10 B-param DiT
  with asymmetric attention (text tokens get cheaper attention);
  Apache-2.0. Strong on motion realism.
- **HunyuanVideo** [@kong2024hunyuanvideo] (Tencent, Dec 2024) —
  13 B-param DiT with a *dual-stream* attention layout (image
  tokens and text tokens are processed in parallel then fused);
  Apache-2.0. The first open model to challenge closed-source quality
  in side-by-side preference tests.
- **Wan 2.1 / Wan 2.2** [@alibaba2025wan] (Alibaba, Feb 2025 /
  Jul 2025) — 14 B-param DiT with high-compression 3D VAE; Apache-2.0.
  Multilingual prompts (English + Chinese) work natively.
- **LTX-Video** [@lightricks2024ltx] (Lightricks, Nov 2024) — 2 B-
  param DiT optimised for *speed*: produces 5-second 768×512 clips
  in 4 seconds on an H100. Trades quality for inference latency in
  the same way SDXL Turbo did for images.
- **Open-Sora / Open-Sora-Plan** [@zheng2024opensora; @lin2024opensoraplan]
  (PKU + HuaWei + community, 2024–2025) — community
  reimplementations of the inferred Sora recipe. Useful for ablations
  and for understanding what a high-quality DiT pipeline looks like
  end-to-end; not yet competitive with the curated commercial models.
- **Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) / SVD-XT / Stable Video 4D**
  [@blattmann2023svd] (Stability AI, 2023–2024) — the U-Net line.
  SVD-XT generates 25-frame clips; Stable Video 4D adds multi-view
  generation (4 views × 8 frames). Still widely used for
  image-to-video where the input is a still image.

The convergence in 2025–2026 is striking: every open generator uses
a **DiT** with a **3D-VAE** latent, **T5-XXL or LLM** text
conditioning, and trains on a **filtered re-captioned video corpus**
(closely mirroring the data evolution of @sec-bench-pretrain in
@sec-video-benchmarks). The differences sit in (i) parameter count,
(ii) attention layout (joint vs dual-stream), (iii) precise VAE
compression ratio, and (iv) inference-time tricks (Mochi's asymmetric
attention, LTX's speed-optimised solver).


## Evaluation {#sec-gen-eval}

Video generation evaluation is in a much worse state than video
understanding evaluation, because there is no single "correct"
output. The 2024–2026 reporting suite is:

### Distributional metrics {.unnumbered}

- **Fréchet Video Distance (FVD)** [@unterthiner2018fvd] (2018). The
  video analogue of FID: compute I3D features for real and generated
  clips, fit Gaussians, measure 2-Wasserstein distance between them.
  Reported on UCF-101 and MSR-VTT. Strong correlation with human
  preference for *content quality*, weak correlation with temporal
  consistency.
- **Inception Score (IS) / Kinetics-FID / CLIP-FID** — variants on
  the FID theme with different feature extractors. Less common in
  2024–2026.

FVD has known issues — sensitive to clip length, frame rate, and the
choice of I3D checkpoint — but it is the only reported number for
nearly every paper, so it persists.

### Compositional / dimension-decomposed metrics {.unnumbered}

- **VBench / VBench++** [@huang2024vbench] (2024). The dominant
  evaluation suite for 2024–2026 generation papers. Breaks down
  generation quality into **16 dimensions** — *subject consistency*,
  *background consistency*, *temporal flickering*, *motion smoothness*,
  *dynamic degree*, *aesthetic quality*, *imaging quality*,
  *object class*, *multiple objects*, *human action*, *colour*,
  *spatial relationship*, *scene*, *appearance style*,
  *temporal style*, *overall consistency* — each scored by a small
  dedicated evaluator (CLIP, ViCLIP, MUSIQ, RAFT, ViT-based
  classifiers). The headline number is a weighted mean; the per-
  dimension breakdown lets papers argue about *which* aspect their
  model is good at.
- **EvalCrafter** [@liu2024evalcrafter] (2024). A similar
  dimension-decomposed benchmark with ~700 prompts × 17 metrics.
  Often reported alongside VBench.
- **VideoScore** [@he2024videoscore] (2024). A learned LLM-based
  evaluator trained on human preference data; emerging as a single-
  number sanity check.

### Human preference {.unnumbered}

Side-by-side preference tests against a strong baseline (typically
Sora, Veo, or CogVideoX-5B). Almost every 2025–2026 paper reports
this in addition to FVD + VBench, because the automatic metrics still
fail to discriminate among the top open models. The standard
protocol: 50–100 prompts × 3–5 raters, blinded A/B comparison, report
win rate.

### Prompt sets {.unnumbered}

The standard ones:

- **VBench prompts** (~950 prompts across the 16 dimensions).
- **EvalCrafter prompts** (~700 prompts).
- **T2V-CompBench** [@sun2024t2vcompbench] — adversarial compositional
  prompts (e.g. *"a red cube on top of a blue cylinder, rotating
  while a yellow ball orbits"*); designed to expose compositional
  failures that pretty pictures hide.

### Recommendations {.unnumbered}

For a 2026 video-generation paper:

1. **FVD on UCF-101 + MSR-VTT** — legacy but expected.
2. **VBench (full 16 dimensions + headline mean)** — the de facto
   2024–2026 default.
3. **A human-preference A/B against a flagship** — Sora 2, Veo 3, or
   CogVideoX 1.5-5B depending on what is fair (closed vs open weights).
4. **Sanity check on a compositional prompt set** (T2V-CompBench or
   one of the VBench compositional sub-axes) — to confirm the model
   has not collapsed to "pretty but wrong".


## Open Problems and Future Directions {#sec-gen-open-problems}

Brief, because the chapter is intentionally short.

- **Long-form video.** Most open models cap out at 5–10 seconds. Sora
  showed 1 min, Veo 3 nominally supports 8 s, Movie Gen ~16 s — but
  *coherent narrative* over a minute is still rare. The open frontier
  is autoregressive *chunked* generation (generate $k$ seconds,
  condition the next chunk on the last) vs *one-shot long-context*
  DiTs.
- **Controllability.** Text alone is a weak control signal for video.
  Pose / depth / camera-trajectory control (Video-ControlNet,
  CameraCtrl), reference-image identity preservation, and structured
  edits (Movie Gen's text-guided editing) are active research lines.
- **Physics.** Top-of-leaderboard models still produce subtle
  physics violations (objects passing through each other, gravity
  glitches, fluid dynamics implausibilities). The 2025–2026 wave of
  *world model* generators (Genie 3, Cosmos) explicitly trades
  generality for physical plausibility.
- **Audio.** Veo 3 and Movie Gen generate synced audio; Sora 2 does
  not yet. Joint video+audio generation is the most likely next
  flagship axis — the model needs to know which sound goes with which
  visible event.
- **Evaluation honesty.** VBench is increasingly *gameable* — papers
  optimise for high VBench scores rather than for human preference.
  The community is working on more adversarial prompt sets
  (T2V-CompBench, Movie Gen Bench) but no clean replacement exists
  yet.


## Summary

Video generation in 2024–2026 has converged on a tight stack: a
**3D-VAE** that compresses pixels to a low-dimensional latent, a
**Diffusion Transformer (DiT)** that denoises that latent, and a
**T5-XXL or LLM text encoder** that injects prompts via
cross-attention. Within that stack, three families differ in how much
*video* training they do — train from scratch (Sora, CogVideoX,
HunyuanVideo), fine-tune from an image model (Make-a-Video, Stable
Video Diffusion), or adapt for free (Text2Video-Zero) — but the
architecture is increasingly the same. The autoregressive line
(VideoPoet, Janus-Pro, MAGI/Cosmos) is the credible orthogonal
alternative, especially for *unified* understanding+generation models.

Compared with video *understanding* (@sec-video-understanding), the
generation field is roughly 18 months behind on data quality and
benchmark consolidation. There is no MVBench-equivalent for generation
in 2026 — VBench is closest, but every paper has its own headline
number and human preference is still the ground truth. As the
infrastructure and data converge, expect the next two years to look
much like the understanding side did in 2024: rapid architectural
convergence, a stable evaluation suite, and a sharper focus on the
remaining hard axes — long form, controllability, physics, and
honest evaluation.

## Interview Questions

**Q: What is the core architectural difference between Sora/CogVideoX and earlier video diffusion models like VDM or Imagen Video?**

VDM and Imagen Video use a U-Net denoiser with 3D convolutions and *factorized* spatiotemporal attention — spatial and temporal processing are largely separate operations. Sora and CogVideoX replace the U-Net with a **Diffusion Transformer (DiT)**, tokenizing the video into 3D spacetime patches and applying full self-attention jointly across all spatial and temporal positions. This lets the same architecture handle variable-length, variable-resolution video (and degenerate to image generation at $T=1$), and benefits from transformer scaling laws — at the cost of higher per-step compute than the factorized U-Net pattern.

---

**Q: Describe how Make-a-Video generates video without training a video diffusion model from scratch.**

Make-a-Video inserts (2D+1) convolutional and attention layers into a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model: each 2D conv is followed by a temporal 1D conv initialized to the identity, and each spatial attention layer is followed by a temporal attention layer. The image weights stay frozen (or lightly fine-tuned); only the new temporal layers are trained on video data. Because the temporal layers initialize as identity functions, the model initially behaves exactly like the image model on individual frames — a stable starting point that preserves image generation quality while learning motion cheaply.

---

**Q: Why does almost every video generator use a 3D VAE rather than the 2D VAE from image diffusion?**

A 2D VAE compresses each frame independently, so a video tensor is still $T$ times larger than a single image latent — the dominant cost for video diffusion. A 3D VAE compresses space *and* time jointly (e.g. $8{\times}8{\times}4$), giving an additional ~4× reduction along the temporal axis on top of the spatial compression. This is what makes it feasible to run a transformer or U-Net over the latent at all; without it, even a modest 16-frame clip would have a sequence length 16× larger than the equivalent image.

---

**Q: VBench reports 16 separate dimensions instead of one number. Why, and what's the risk?**

Video quality is multi-axis: a model can have excellent per-frame aesthetics but flicker badly (low temporal consistency), or move very little because static frames score well on most metrics (low "dynamic degree"). A single averaged score hides these trade-offs and can be gamed — e.g., a model that barely moves scores well on subject/background consistency. The 16-dimension breakdown lets a paper show *which* axis it improves, but the flip side is that papers increasingly optimize directly for VBench sub-scores rather than for human preference, which is why human A/B testing remains mandatory alongside it.

---

**Q: Compare the autoregressive and diffusion approaches to video generation. Why might unification with LLMs matter beyond raw quality?**

Diffusion generates a clip by iterative denoising of a continuous (or VAE) latent and currently leads on raw visual quality (Sora, Veo 3, CogVideoX 1.5). Autoregressive generation tokenizes video into discrete VQ codes and predicts them one at a time, like text — currently behind on quality but improving rapidly with better tokenizers (MAGVIT-v2). The unification argument is architectural: an AR video model uses the *same* token interface as an LLM, so a single transformer can both understand video (read tokens, write text — Chapter 11) and generate it (read text, write tokens), and inherits every LLM-serving optimization (speculative decoding, KV-cache reuse, prefix sharing) for free. This is why Janus-Pro and the broader "unified" model line bet on AR despite the current quality gap.

---

**Q: How does classifier-free guidance behave differently for video versus image generation?**

CFG blends conditional and unconditional denoiser outputs, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} = \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing) + w[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{c}) - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing)]$, trading diversity for prompt fidelity. For video, the practical guidance scale is typically higher (6–9 vs. 4–7.5 for images) because the temporal-consistency requirement makes under-conditioned samples noticeably worse — a video that drifts off-prompt over time looks like a different video halfway through, which is far more jarring than a single off-prompt image. Over-guidance also has a video-specific failure mode: oversaturated, low-motion ("frozen") clips, since high guidance pushes toward the conditional mode at the expense of the diversity that produces natural motion.
